analysis.one_liner: Caps how big and how leveraged any single bank can be, to end "too big to fail."
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on April 28, 2010 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put a hard ceiling on bank size: no bank holding company could hold more than 10% of the nation's insured deposits, and banks would have to sell assets to comply. It would have required banks and large financial companies to hold a cushion of at least 6 cents of capital per dollar of assets and debts, capped how much banks could borrow outside deposits (2% of GDP for bank holding companies, 3% for nonbank financial companies), and ordered the SEC to force companies to put all their assets and debts on their balance sheets instead of hiding them off the books. The goal was to make sure no bank is so large or so leveraged that its failure forces taxpayers to bail it out. It never got a hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, who bore the cost of the 2008 bailouts, would benefit from a banking system in which no single company is large enough or leveraged enough to threaten the economy's stability if it fails. Smaller and regional banks would also gain market share if the giants were forced to shrink. savers and borrowers would face a system less prone to crisis-driven credit freezes.

how_it_helps.text: It caps any single bank holding company at 10% of all U.S. insured deposits and requires the Federal Reserve to force violators to sell assets — directly shrinking the biggest banks.
It requires banks and large financial companies to hold at least 6% capital against their assets and liabilities, giving them a thicker cushion against losses so failures are less likely to cascade.

It caps nondeposit borrowing at 2% of GDP for bank holding companies and 3% for nonbank financial companies, counting off-balance-sheet debts — closing the accounting loopholes that let firms like Lehman Brothers hide leverage.
It directs the SEC to require companies to record all assets and liabilities on their balance sheets, so investors and regulators can actually see what a firm owes.

analysis.who_pays: The largest bank holding companies and big nonbank financial companies, which would have to sell assets, raise capital, and shrink to meet the deposit cap, the 6% leverage minimums, and the limits on nondeposit borrowing within one to three years. Their shareholders would absorb the cost of restructuring.
analysis.who_pays_short: The biggest banks and financial firms

drawbacks.text: Institutions out of compliance would have had as little as one year to meet the new leverage ratios and deposit cap (three years for liability limits), which could force rapid asset sales and tighten credit in the middle of a fragile recovery.

The 6% leverage ratio applied uniformly regardless of how risky a bank's assets were, and while regulators could grant emergency temporary exemptions, that flexibility is discretionary and temporary rather than built into the standard.

The bill's liability caps cover bank holding companies and nonbank financial companies supervised by the Federal Reserve, so financial activity could migrate toward entities outside those definitions; the bill also gives regulators authority to set separate limits for insurance companies and to exclude some foreign deposits from the calculation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside was real: hard limits on bank size and leverage would have directly attacked the "too big to fail" problem that forced taxpayers to bail out the banking system in 2008, and the bill included safeguards — emergency exemptions for financial stability, phase-in periods, and off-balance-sheet reporting — against the harshest adjustment scenarios. The honest costs: as little as one year to meet the leverage and deposit caps could have forced rapid asset sales and tightened credit, and a flat 6% ratio ignores risk differences across banks. On balance the bill was a serious, if blunt, attempt to fix a problem that costs ordinary people dearly when it goes wrong, and it was never even given a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Miller of North Carolina introduced the bill on April 28, 2010, joined by four original cosponsors — Reps. Chandler, Cohen, Ellison, and Sherman.
The bill would cap any bank holding company at 10% of all U.S. insured deposits and require the Federal Reserve to force noncompliant firms to sell assets to get under the limit.

It would set minimum 6% leverage ratios for bank holding companies and large financial companies, and cap nondeposit liabilities at 2% of GDP for bank holding companies and 3% of GDP for nonbank financial companies, counting off-balance-sheet obligations.
It would also require the SEC to write rules putting all assets and liabilities on companies' balance sheets, closing the off-balance-sheet accounting gap that hid risk before the 2008 crisis.

The House referred the bill to the Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced; the committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest bank holding companies and nonbank financial companies, which faced no new caps on their size, leverage, or off-balance-sheet borrowing. Congress passed the Dodd-Frank financial law that year without these hard size limits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest banks and financial firms

for.name: Rep. Brad Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 28, 2010 to cap bank size, leverage, and nondeposit liabilities.

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to on April 28, 2010; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: The largest U.S. bank holding companies
against.role: Wall Street banks during the 2010 financial-regulation debate
against.what_they_did: Fought hard limits on bank size and leverage during the Dodd-Frank debate, lobbying for capital rules and resolution authority instead of breakup requirements.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split was recorded; the sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill stalled in a committee chaired by a member of the same majority party.

industries.note: The bill would force the biggest banks — already near or past the 10% deposit share — to divest deposits and shrink, and would raise their capital requirements. Smaller banks mean less systemic risk for taxpayers and depositors, but the megabanks' size gave them lobbying weight the bill never overcame.

industries.industry: Nonbank financial companies (investment firms, insurers with financial operations)
industries.note: For the first time, nonbank financial companies would face a hard cap on nondeposit liabilities at 3% of GDP plus leverage minimums. This targets the 'shadow banking' sector whose hidden leverage helped cause the 2008 crisis.

A binding cap on any one company's deposit share would preserve market share for regional and community banks. Their competitive interest roughly runs alongside the public's interest in a less concentrated banking system.
